quiz.prompt: Four learners will each group the same 13 organisms (maize, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat). Amina uses size, Brian uses colour, Cheche uses where the organism lives, and Dennis uses whether people eat it. What is the most reasonable prediction about their groupings?
choices: The groupings will match as long as the learners work in the same classroom
The groupings will probably differ because each learner is using a different rule
All four groupings will be exactly the same because the organisms are the same
Only Amina's grouping can work because size is always easy to measure
quiz.rationale: Each learner uses a different personal rule (size, colour, habitat, food value), so different groupings are expected even though the organisms are the same.
quiz.placement: Predict: learners write a prediction on how many groups, what rule, and whether their groups would match their neighbour's

quiz.prompt: During the observation of the 13 organisms, learners must record features they can see for themselves. Which of these is an observable feature of the butterfly?
choices: It is less important than the goat
It has wings
It is harmful to people
It is useful as food
quiz.rationale: Having wings can be seen directly by looking at the butterfly. Harmful, useful as food and importance are opinions or uses, not observed body features.
quiz.placement: Observe: learners record at least two observable features for each of the 13 organisms

quiz.prompt: While grouping the organisms, a learner says: 'The mushroom is a plant because it grows in soil.' At this point in the lesson, what is the best response from the teacher?
choices: Point out that 'grows in soil' is a habitat-based rule, and ask what observable features of the mushroom could be compared with the other organisms
Say that the mushroom is an animal because it cannot move
Agree, because anything that grows in soil is a plant
Tell the learner to stop asking about the mushroom
quiz.rationale: Where an organism lives is only one everyday rule. The teacher should push learners to give observable features as evidence, and the mushroom's group is left as a question to explore in later lessons.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher asks 'Why did you put the mushroom with the plants? What made you decide that?'

quiz.prompt: One group places the goat and the chicken together under the title 'farm animals'. Another group places them in different groups because the goat has hair and the chicken has feathers. Both groups were looking at the same two organisms. Why did their groupings differ?
choices: The two groups used different rules to make their groups
One group made a mistake in observing and the other group observed correctly
Groupings differ only when learners come from different counties
The goat and the chicken are not both living things
quiz.rationale: The first group used usefulness or where the animals are kept, while the second used body covering. The different results come from the different rules, not from wrong observation.
quiz.placement: Explain: gallery walk comparing groupings by colour, size, habitat or usefulness

quiz.prompt: After the gallery walk, a learner from Kericho says: 'I can use your group's manila paper to place the mushroom exactly where you did.' Your group grouped by 'what looks useful to us'. Why might the learner from Kericho not get the same result?
choices: Because groupings only work in the school where they were made
Because people in Kericho cannot see the same organisms
Because the mushroom cannot be grouped at all
Because a rule such as 'useful to us' can mean different things to different people, so the groupings will not match
quiz.rationale: Rules such as usefulness, colour or size are judged differently by different people. This shows why a standard system based on shared, observable characteristics is needed, so anyone anywhere gets the same result.
quiz.placement: Explain: Think-Pair-Share 'Why do scientists need a standard system of classification?'

quiz.prompt: The class is adding questions to the Driving Question Board under 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' Which question fits best on this board?
choices: Which organism in the display is the cheapest to buy?
How do scientists decide which features to use when they classify organisms?
Which organism in the display is the biggest?
Which group made the neatest manila paper?
quiz.rationale: This question is directly about the process of classification and about choosing characteristics. It is the kind of question that leads to the next lesson. The other questions are about size, price or neatness.
quiz.placement: DQB: learners post questions under the driving question 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?'

quiz.prompt: For the exit ticket, a learner must give one observable characteristic that could be used to group the maize, the bean plant and the grass together. Which answer is the best?
choices: They are all eaten by people
They all grow in Kisumu
They all have leaves and roots
They are all exactly the same size
quiz.rationale: Having leaves and roots is an observable feature shared by all three. Grass is not normally eaten by people, the three differ in size, and growing in Kisumu is not a body feature.
quiz.placement: Model: exit ticket (b) give one observable characteristic to group the maize, bean plant and grass together

quiz.prompt: Before examining moss, a learner predicts: "Moss is like maize. It has true roots and flowers." Which statement about moss is correct?
choices: Moss is a fungus, like a mushroom, so it has no green parts
Moss has true roots, but they are shorter than those of maize
Moss has no flowers and reproduces using spores, not seeds
Moss has flowers but they are too small to see
quiz.rationale: Mosses (Division Bryophyta) have no flowers, no seeds and no true roots. They reproduce by spores formed in capsules. They are green plants, not fungi.
quiz.placement: Predict: private prediction sheet and Think-Pair-Share on 'Is moss more like maize, grass, or fern?'

quiz.prompt: A learner looks at the base of a moss plant with a hand lens and sees many thin, thread-like structures going into the soil. What are they and what is their main job?
choices: Rhizoids that anchor the plant
True roots that carry water up through xylem
Root hairs that carry food down through phloem
Spore capsules that release spores into the soil
quiz.rationale: Moss has rhizoids, not true roots. They mainly anchor the plant and do not transport water like the true roots of maize.
quiz.placement: Observe: hand-lens examination of the moss base and comparison with the maize or bean root

quiz.prompt: A group makes a labelled biological drawing of one moss plant. Which drawing is done correctly?
choices: It is shaded to show colour, with label lines that cross each other so all labels fit
It has curved label lines drawn over the structures to show exactly where each part is
It has a title and magnification, uses a sharp pencil with single clear lines, and has straight label lines that do not cross
It has no title, so the drawing looks neat and uncluttered
quiz.rationale: A good biological drawing has a title and magnification, clear single lines with no shading, and straight label lines that do not cross.
quiz.placement: Observe: labelled drawing of one moss plant with title, magnification and label lines

quiz.prompt: A group compares moss with a maize seedling in a table. Which row of differences is correct?
choices: Moss: large size and true leaves. Maize: very small size and no leaves.
Moss: flowers and seeds. Maize: spore capsules on stalks.
Moss: rhizoids, no vascular tissue, spore capsules. Maize: true roots, xylem and phloem, seeds.
Moss: true roots and xylem. Maize: rhizoids and no vascular tissue.
quiz.rationale: Moss has rhizoids, lacks xylem and phloem, and makes spores in capsules. Maize has true roots, vascular tissue and seeds. The other rows swap or invent features.
quiz.placement: Observe: table with columns Feature | Moss | Maize/Bean | Fern

quiz.prompt: Maize carries water up its stem through xylem. Moss has no xylem or phloem. What does this lack of vascular tissue tell us about moss?
choices: It grows tall in dry places because it does not need water
It cannot make food because it has no phloem
It stays small because it has too many rhizoids
It stays small because it cannot transport water and food over long distances
quiz.rationale: Without xylem and phloem, water and food cannot be moved efficiently over long distances. Moss therefore stays small and lives where water is easily available. It still makes its own food by photosynthesis.
quiz.placement: Explain: Think-Pair-Share 'Why does moss stay small and grow only in damp places?'

quiz.prompt: A learner finds moss growing on a damp, shaded wall in Nairobi, but none on a dry, sunny rock nearby. Which statement best explains this and how the moss reproduces?
choices: Moss needs deep true roots to reach water, so it grows only on walls
Moss needs bright sunshine to form seeds, so it avoids the dry rock
Moss reproduces by flowers that open only in shade
Moss needs water for fertilisation and has no vascular tissue to bring water from far away, so it lives in damp places and reproduces by spores
quiz.rationale: Bryophytes need water for fertilisation and cannot transport water far without vascular tissue. They make spores in capsules on stalks, not seeds or flowers.
quiz.placement: Explain: 'How does it reproduce without seeds or flowers?' and the link to damp places near Kericho and Nairobi

quiz.prompt: A group is adding a 'Bryophyta' category to its classification model. Which criterion is most useful for deciding whether a plant belongs in the group?
choices: It has no true roots, stems or leaves, has rhizoids, and bears spore capsules on stalks
It is green in colour
It is not used as food by people
It is small enough to fit in your hand
quiz.rationale: Groups should be defined by shared, observable structural features. Colour, size alone and usefulness do not separate moss from other plants, since maize and fern are also green.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the Lesson 1 classification chart with a 'Bryophyta' category and criteria

quiz.prompt: A learner turns over a fern frond and sees rows of small brown dots on the underside. What are these brown dots?
choices: Flowers that have dried up
Eggs laid by insects
Seeds ready to be planted
Sori, which hold spores for reproduction
quiz.rationale: Brown dots on the underside of a fern frond are sori, which contain spores. Ferns reproduce by spores and make no seeds or flowers.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw, Part 1: Reproductive structures expert group examining the underside of the fern frond

quiz.prompt: A learner pulls up a maize plant and a bean plant and examines their roots. Which description is correct?
choices: Both have rhizoids instead of true roots
Maize has fibrous roots and bean has a tap root
Both have a rhizome with fibrous roots
Maize has a tap root and bean has fibrous roots
quiz.rationale: Maize has fibrous roots and bean has a tap root. Rhizoids belong to moss, and a rhizome with fibrous roots belongs to the fern.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw, Part 1: Roots expert group (fibrous vs tap root vs rhizome vs rhizoids)

quiz.prompt: A learner examines a leaf that is broad and has veins forming a net pattern. Which plant did the leaf most likely come from?
choices: Fern
Bean plant
Maize plant
Moss
quiz.rationale: Bean leaves are broad with net veins. Maize leaves are long and narrow with parallel veins, and ferns have fronds with pinnae.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw, Part 1: Leaves expert group (counting veins: parallel or net)

quiz.prompt: A home group is completing its comparison table. Which feature separates a fern (Pteridophyta) from moss (Bryophyta)?
choices: The fern makes seeds but moss makes spores
The fern has rhizoids only, but moss has true roots
The fern has flowers but moss does not
The fern has true roots and vascular tissue, but moss does not
quiz.rationale: Ferns have true roots, stems, leaves (fronds) and vascular tissue. Moss lacks true roots and vascular tissue. Ferns do not make seeds or flowers.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw, Part 2: home groups build the comparison table (Bryophyta | Pteridophyta | Spermatophyta)

quiz.prompt: A learner says, "Ferns are flowering plants, so they make seeds." Which evidence from the specimens shows this is wrong?
choices: A fern has no roots, so it cannot make seeds
A fern frond has sori with spores on the underside, and it has no flowers or seeds
A fern frond is green, and only plants with other colours make seeds
A fern frond is smaller than a bean plant, so it makes no seeds
quiz.rationale: Ferns reproduce by spores held in sori and do not have flowers or seeds. Ferns do have true roots, and size and colour are not used to decide how a plant reproduces.
quiz.placement: Gallery walk and class discussion: revisiting the prediction 'ferns have flowers'

quiz.prompt: Both ferns and bean plants have vascular tissue, true roots, stems and leaves. Which feature best separates a fern from a bean plant?
choices: A fern reproduces by seeds in pods, while a bean plant reproduces by spores
A bean plant has rhizoids, but a fern has true roots
A fern has vascular tissue, but a bean plant does not
A fern reproduces by spores in sori, while a bean plant reproduces by seeds
quiz.rationale: Both groups have vascular tissue and true roots, so these do not separate them. Ferns reproduce by spores and spermatophytes such as beans reproduce by seeds.
quiz.placement: Notebook sentences: 'The feature that best separates a fern from a bean plant is ___ because ___'

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kericho and a student in Kisumu both want to place a plant in the same group. Why is checking for spores or seeds better than grouping by size or colour?
choices: Spores and seeds are always bigger than the plant parts that show colour
Only scientists are allowed to look for spores and seeds
Size and colour never change, but spores and seeds do
Anyone can observe and check spores or seeds in the same way, so people reach the same grouping
quiz.rationale: Classification needs shared, observable features that anyone can check and agree on. Size, colour or use as food differ from person to person, which is why learners' own groupings disagreed.
quiz.placement: Class discussion: 'Would a farmer in Kericho and a student in Kisumu both be able to check spores and seeds?'

quiz.prompt: In the class flow chart, the first question is "Vascular tissue?" A plant answers "Yes", and the second question is "Seeds?" The plant answers "No, it makes spores". Which group does it belong to?
choices: Pteridophyta (fern)
Bryophyta (moss)
Spermatophyta (maize, bean)
It is not a plant, like the mushroom
quiz.rationale: A plant with vascular tissue that reproduces by spores and has no seeds is a pteridophyte, such as a fern. Moss has no vascular tissue, and spermatophytes make seeds.
quiz.placement: Revising the class model (flow chart): Vascular tissue? then Seeds? to place moss, fern, maize and bean

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kericho cannot ask you for help, but she must name a plant using only your written instructions. Which first step would most likely give her the same answer you get?
choices: Is the plant big or small?
Is the plant useful as food?
Is the plant a pretty colour?
Does the leaf have parallel veins or net-like veins?
quiz.rationale: Vein pattern is a visible feature that anyone can check and that does not change with opinion. Size, usefulness and prettiness depend on the person, so different people would answer differently.
quiz.placement: Predict: writing instructions so a farmer in Kericho gets the same name for a plant

quiz.prompt: The first couplet of a key says: 1a: Plant has no true roots, stems or leaves. 1b: Plant has true roots, stems and leaves. Which plant belongs at 1a?
choices: Bean plant
Fern
Maize plant
Moss
quiz.rationale: Moss (Bryophyta) has no true roots, stems or leaves, so it fits 1a. Fern, bean and maize all have true roots, stems and leaves and fit 1b.
quiz.placement: Part A: reading the first couplet of the sample key and modelling it with moss

quiz.prompt: A learner lays a ruler beside a sukuma wiki leaf. The base of the leaf is at the 2 cm mark and the tip is at the 14 cm mark. What is the length of the leaf?
choices: 14 cm
2 cm
12 cm
16 cm
quiz.rationale: The leaf does not start at zero, so subtract the start reading from the end reading: 14 cm - 2 cm = 12 cm.
quiz.placement: Part B: measuring features such as leaf length with rulers while using the key outside

quiz.prompt: Different groups used the same key on the same plants and got the same names. Their own earlier groupings by size, colour and usefulness did not agree. Why did the key give the same answer to everyone?
choices: It uses pairs of contrasting, observable features, so each person makes the same clear choice at each step.
It lets each person choose any number of statements that they like.
It uses the colour of the plant, which is the same for all people.
It groups plants by how useful they are, which everyone agrees on.
quiz.rationale: A key works for everyone because each couplet offers two contrasting statements about features that can be seen or measured. Colour, size and usefulness depend on opinion, so they gave different groupings.
quiz.placement: Step 1: Think-Pair-Share on why the key gave the same answer to different people

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the best couplet to include in a dichotomous key for plants?
choices: 1a: Leaf has parallel veins. 1b: Leaf has net-like veins.
1a: Plant is useful. 1b: Plant is not useful.
1a: Plant is beautiful. 1b: Plant is not beautiful.
1a: Leaf is green. 1b: Leaf is dark green.
quiz.rationale: A good couplet has two contrasting statements about observable features, and only one can be chosen. Parallel veins and net-like veins meet this rule. Usefulness and beauty are opinions, and green versus dark green do not clearly contrast.
quiz.placement: Step 2: listing what makes each couplet good and building the principles of construction

quiz.prompt: A group is building a key for a maize plant, a grass plant, a bean plant and a sukuma wiki plant. They find that the leaves of maize and grass have parallel veins. To which group do maize and grass belong?
choices: Dicots, because they are in Spermatophyta
Pteridophyta, because they have long leaves
Monocots, because parallel veins are a monocot feature
Bryophyta, because they are small green plants
quiz.rationale: Parallel veins are a feature of monocots such as maize and grass. Bean and sukuma wiki have net-like veins and are dicots. Bryophyta and Pteridophyta are different divisions with no seeds.
quiz.placement: Step 3: Dichotomous-key Challenge, linking features to Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, monocots and dicots

quiz.prompt: A group revises its classification model after using the key. Their old model has a group called 'plants that are good to eat'. What is the best revision?
choices: Make the 'good to eat' group larger by adding more plants.
Cross out the group and replace it with observable features such as parallel or net-like veins.
Colour the group in red so that it stands out.
Keep the group, because food use is the most important feature of a plant.
quiz.rationale: Being good to eat is an opinion or use, not an observable feature, so different people group plants differently. Observable features give groups that anyone can check and that fit the key.
quiz.placement: Model revision: crossing out or relabelling groupings based on opinion, such as 'good to eat'

quiz.prompt: In a class activity, groups sorted eight animal pictures. One group sorted by size, another by 'animals we eat', and a third by habitat. A scientist in Nairobi and one in Kisumu need to agree on how to group animals. What is the main problem with these sorting rules?
choices: They depend on opinion or situation, so different people get different groups
They cannot be written on manila paper
They only work for animals that live on land
They use too many animals at once
quiz.rationale: Size, food use and habitat vary with the person or place, so groupings differ. Scientists need shared, observable features that give the same result for everyone.
quiz.placement: Predict: sorting the animal picture cards and recording rules on the board

quiz.prompt: A learner says, 'A snail and an earthworm are both soft-bodied, so they must belong to the same phylum.' Which observation best shows the snail is NOT in the same phylum as the earthworm?
choices: The snail is smaller than the earthworm
The snail is found in gardens, while the earthworm lives in soil
The snail has a hard shell and an unsegmented body, while the earthworm has a body divided into many rings
The snail moves more slowly than the earthworm
quiz.rationale: Snails (Mollusca) have a soft unsegmented body with a shell, while earthworms (Annelida) have a segmented body with rings. Size, speed and habitat are not phylum features.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert A group (Annelida and Mollusca: earthworm, snail)

quiz.prompt: A mosquito has three body parts, six jointed legs and a hard outer covering. Which phylum does it belong to?
choices: Chordata
Arthropoda
Annelida
Mollusca
quiz.rationale: Jointed legs and a hard exoskeleton are features of Arthropoda. The mosquito has no backbone, no shell and no body rings.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert B group (Arthropoda: butterfly, mosquito, grasshopper)

quiz.prompt: A tilapia from Lake Victoria, a lizard, a chicken and a goat all look very different. Which feature do they ALL share that places them in the same phylum?
choices: Living in water
A backbone
Scales covering the body
Wings for flying
quiz.rationale: Chordata in this lesson are the animals with a backbone (fish, reptiles, birds, mammals). Their body coverings, habitats and movement differ.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert D and Expert E groups (Chordata: tilapia, lizard, chicken, goat)

quiz.prompt: A learner writes this claim: 'The butterfly belongs to Phylum Arthropoda.' Which piece of evidence best supports the claim?
choices: It is found in the school garden
It has jointed legs and an exoskeleton
It is useful for pollinating flowers
It is beautiful and colourful
quiz.rationale: Good evidence is an observable body feature that anyone can check. Jointed legs and an exoskeleton are Arthropoda features, while the other options are opinion, habitat or usefulness.
quiz.placement: Explain: writing Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statements for chosen animals

quiz.prompt: A mosquito feeds on blood and a goat feeds on grass, yet they are placed in different phyla. Which is the best reason?
choices: The mosquito can fly but the goat cannot
The mosquito has jointed legs and an exoskeleton with no backbone, while the goat has a backbone
The mosquito is smaller than the goat
The mosquito feeds on blood but the goat does not
quiz.rationale: Phyla are decided by body features such as a backbone, jointed legs and exoskeleton. The mosquito is an arthropod and the goat is a chordate. Size, feeding and flight are not used to decide phylum.
quiz.placement: Explain: comparing why the mosquito and goat are in different phyla

quiz.prompt: A class is building a tree diagram of Kingdom Animalia. Which animal is placed correctly under its phylum?
choices: Butterfly under Chordata, because it can fly
Lizard under Mollusca, because it is cold to touch
Earthworm under Annelida, because its body is divided into rings and it has no legs
Snail under Arthropoda, because it has a hard shell
quiz.rationale: The earthworm's segmented body with no legs places it in Annelida. The snail is Mollusca, the lizard is Chordata and the butterfly is Arthropoda.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the class classification tree diagram with phyla and distinguishing features

quiz.prompt: A goat, a chicken and a lizard are all in Phylum Chordata. Which observable feature can be used to place the chicken in a different class from the goat?
choices: The chicken and the goat are both used as food
The chicken is smaller than the goat
The chicken is usually white or brown in colour
The chicken has feathers, while the goat has hair
quiz.rationale: Classes are separated by structural features such as body covering. Feathers belong to birds (Aves) and hair belongs to mammals (Mammalia). Size, colour and use as food are the learners' own groupings and are not shared, reliable features.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on which features could split the chicken, lizard and goat into smaller groups

quiz.prompt: A student examines a dead mosquito and a spider. Which statement correctly describes the mosquito and its class?
choices: It has three pairs of legs and a body in three parts, so it belongs to Insecta
It has three pairs of legs and feathers, so it belongs to Aves
It has four pairs of legs and belongs to Arachnida
It has no legs and belongs to Crustacea
quiz.rationale: Insects such as the mosquito have six legs (three pairs), antennae and three body parts. Spiders have eight legs (four pairs) and belong to Arachnida. Counting legs corrects the error that insects have 8 legs.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Part 1: Arthropoda classes expert group (dead mosquito and butterfly, spider picture)

quiz.prompt: A bat can fly. It has hair on its body, feeds its young on milk and gives birth to live young. To which class does a bat belong?
choices: Insecta, because it has wings
Mammalia, because of its hair, milk and live young
Reptilia, because it has a dry body covering
Aves, because it can fly
quiz.rationale: Class is decided by features such as body covering and reproduction, not by ability to fly. Hair, milk and live young show that a bat is a mammal. Birds are defined by feathers.
quiz.placement: Step 2: CER response 'Is a bat a bird or a mammal?'

quiz.prompt: A group writes this key: 1a. Has feathers – Aves; 1b. No feathers – go to 2. 2a. Has hair – Mammalia; 2b. No hair – go to 3. 3a. Has dry, scaly skin – Reptilia; 3b. Has moist skin – Amphibia. Which animal follows 1b, then 2b, then 3a?
choices: A frog
A goat
A chicken
A lizard
quiz.rationale: A lizard has no feathers, no hair and has dry, scaly skin, so it ends at Reptilia. A chicken stops at 1a, a goat at 2a, and a frog goes to 3b.
quiz.placement: Step 1: Dichotomous-key challenge, groups swap and test keys

quiz.prompt: Which feature separates reptiles from amphibians?
choices: Amphibians have hair, but reptiles do not
Reptiles have feathers, but amphibians do not
Reptiles have dry, scaly skin, but amphibians have moist skin without scales
Reptiles have gills as adults, but amphibians have lungs
quiz.rationale: Reptiles such as the lizard have dry, scaly skin. Amphibians such as frogs have moist skin without scales. Feathers belong to birds and hair belongs to mammals.
quiz.placement: Exit check: 'Name one feature that separates reptiles from amphibians'

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes how phyla and classes are related in classifying animals?
choices: Classes are made by grouping animals by size and colour
Classes are larger groups that contain several phyla
A phylum is a broad group that is divided into classes using more specific characteristics
Phyla and classes are the same thing and use the same features
quiz.rationale: A phylum such as Chordata is broad, so it is divided into classes (Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia) using features like body covering, limbs, respiration and reproduction. This is the new idea added to the Driving Question Board.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: sticky notes on what we learned about classes of animals

quiz.prompt: When updating a classification model, a group must place a snail. Where does it belong?
choices: In neither Chordata nor Arthropoda, because it belongs to another phylum
In Phylum Arthropoda, because it has a hard shell
In Phylum Chordata, class Reptilia, because it moves slowly
In Class Insecta, because it is a small animal
quiz.rationale: A snail is an animal but is not a chordate or an arthropod. It belongs to a different phylum, so it is marked separately on the model. A shell is not the same as an arthropod's jointed legs and exoskeleton.
quiz.placement: Revising the class classification model on manila paper: placing the phenomenon animals on branches

lessons.title: Dichotomous keys for animals and viruses

quiz.prompt: A visitor from Kisumu has never seen the animals at your school. You can only send a written message so that the visitor names the same animal as you. Which statement would work best in the message?
choices: It is a beautiful animal.
It is a big animal.
It has six jointed legs.
It is a useful animal for food.
quiz.rationale: Six jointed legs is a feature anyone can see and count, so everyone reads it the same way. Big, beautiful and useful are opinions that differ between people.
quiz.placement: Predict: message to a visitor from Kisumu (what kind of statements would work best)

quiz.prompt:
A group builds this part of a dichotomous key.
1a. Animal has a backbone: go to step 2.
1b. Animal has no backbone: go to step 3.
2a. Feathers present: chicken.
2b. Feathers absent, hair present: goat.
3a. Six jointed legs present: grasshopper.
3b. No legs, body covered by a hard shell: snail.
A tester has an animal with no backbone and six jointed legs. Which animal does the key lead to?
choices: Goat
Grasshopper
Chicken
Snail
quiz.rationale: No backbone leads to step 3, and six jointed legs leads to grasshopper. Following one choice at each step gives one answer.
quiz.placement: Part A: swapping keys and identifying mystery animals

quiz.prompt: A group wrote this couplet: 'Animal is small' / 'Animal is big'. After swapping keys, the testing group got different answers from the authors. What is the main problem with this couplet?
choices: Animals never differ in size, so the feature is useless.
The couplet should name the animal in the first statement.
A couplet must have three choices, not two.
Two people can disagree about what small and big mean, because the statements are not measurable or countable.
quiz.rationale: Small and big depend on what each person compares with. A good couplet uses observable, countable features, such as a backbone or the number of legs, so every user reaches the same answer.
quiz.placement: Part A: group records where the key failed or was ambiguous and fixes it

quiz.prompt: Learners sort animals into Phylum Chordata or Phylum Arthropoda. Which list contains only Arthropoda?
choices: Chicken, lizard, grasshopper
Butterfly, earthworm, grasshopper
Mosquito, butterfly, grasshopper
Mosquito, butterfly, snail
quiz.rationale: Mosquito, butterfly and grasshopper are insects with jointed legs, so they are Arthropoda. The snail and earthworm are neither Arthropoda nor Chordata. Chicken and lizard are Chordata.
quiz.placement: Part A: compare with the prepared key and sort animals into Chordata or Arthropoda

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a virus?
choices: It has a nucleus and mitochondria, like the cells of a goat.
It is a very small bacterium that divides on its own in soil.
It is a non-cellular particle with a protein coat around DNA or RNA, and it reproduces only inside a host cell.
It carries out respiration and growth by itself outside a host.
quiz.rationale: Viruses have no cell structure and no nucleus or mitochondria. They have genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat and can reproduce only inside a host cell.
quiz.placement: Part B: virus diagrams and reading, table of virus characteristics

quiz.prompt: A learner claims that a virus is not a living organism. Which piece of evidence best supports this claim?
choices: A virus has genetic material, DNA or RNA.
A virus can cause disease in maize and in people.
A virus is very small.
A virus has no cell structure and cannot reproduce or carry out metabolism outside a host cell.
quiz.rationale: Living things show characteristics such as reproduction and metabolism on their own. A virus has no cells and depends on a host cell for these. Small size, causing disease and having genetic material do not show that something is non-living.
quiz.placement: CER: 'Is a virus a living organism?'

quiz.prompt: A health worker says that antibiotics will not cure measles. What is the correct reason?
choices: Measles is caused by a very large bacterium that resists antibiotics.
Antibiotics only work on diseases of plants.
Measles is not caused by any organism or particle.
Measles is caused by a virus, which is not a bacterium, and antibiotics work against bacteria.
quiz.rationale: Viruses are non-cellular particles that live and reproduce inside host cells, and they are not bacteria. Antibiotics target bacteria, so vaccines are used to prevent virus diseases like measles.
quiz.placement: Teacher probe: correct the misconceptions 'viruses are tiny bacteria' and 'antibiotics kill viruses'

quiz.prompt: Learners add a box for viruses to the class model. Which example shows a useful (beneficial) importance of viruses?
choices: Bacteriophages being used to attack harmful bacteria
Cassava mosaic disease reducing cassava yields on Kenyan farms
Foot and mouth disease in cattle
Newcastle disease killing chickens
quiz.rationale: Bacteriophages are viruses that infect and destroy bacteria, so they can be used against harmful bacteria. The other three examples are harmful viral diseases of crops and livestock.
quiz.placement: Revise the class model: add a box for viruses showing their importance in health, agriculture and biotechnology

quiz.prompt: Learners from a school in Kisumu receive 6 unfamiliar organisms and must group them exactly as a school in Kericho does. What would help them most to get the same groups?
choices: Use the same observable characteristics and a shared dichotomous key
Group them by size, from the biggest to the smallest
Group them by how useful each one is as food
Group them by colour so that similar-looking ones are together
quiz.rationale: Shared, observable characteristics and a key let any learner reach the same groups. Size, colour and use as food vary from person to person and give different groupings, as seen in Lesson 1.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share prediction on classifying 6 unfamiliar organisms from Kericho, Kisumu or Mombasa

quiz.prompt: Why are viruses not placed in Kingdom Plantae or Kingdom Animalia?
choices: Viruses are too small to be seen with any instrument
Viruses are not made of cells, so they do not fit into either kingdom
Viruses only live in water and not on land
Viruses are single cells that have no nucleus
quiz.rationale: Viruses are non-cellular. Plants and animals are made of cells, so viruses cannot be placed in either kingdom. The idea that 'viruses are cells' is a common misconception.
quiz.placement: Final classification challenge: one-line note on viruses (why they are not placed in either kingdom)

quiz.prompt: A fern is in Division Pteridophyta and moss is in Division Bryophyta. Which feature separates the fern from the moss?
choices: The fern has vascular tissue, but the moss does not
The moss makes seeds, but the fern makes spores
The fern has flowers, but the moss does not
The moss has vascular tissue, but the fern does not
quiz.rationale: Ferns have vascular tissue and reproduce by spores. Mosses lack vascular tissue. Neither makes seeds or flowers.
quiz.placement: Final classification challenge, Task 1: sorting cards into Divisions (Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Spermatophyta)

quiz.prompt: A plant has seeds enclosed in a fruit, leaves with net veins, and seeds with two cotyledons. Which group does it belong to?
choices: Gymnospermae
Bryophyta
Angiospermae, dicotyledon
Angiospermae, monocotyledon
quiz.rationale: Seeds enclosed in a fruit mean Angiospermae. Net veins and two cotyledons mean a dicotyledon, like the bean. Maize has parallel veins and one cotyledon, so it is a monocotyledon.
quiz.placement: Final classification challenge, Task 1: sorting maize and bean into monocot and dicot

quiz.prompt: A mosquito has a jointed exoskeleton, three pairs of jointed legs and no backbone. Which phylum does it belong to, and why?
choices: Arthropoda, because it is small and harmful to people
Chordata, because it is an animal that can fly
Arthropoda, because it has a jointed exoskeleton and jointed legs
Chordata, because it has three pairs of legs
quiz.rationale: Arthropods have a jointed exoskeleton and jointed legs. Chordates have a backbone, which the mosquito lacks. Size and harmfulness are not classification characteristics.
quiz.placement: Final classification challenge, Task 1: sorting into Phyla and Classes (Chordata and Arthropoda)

quiz.prompt: Which pair of statements is best for one step in a dichotomous key for insects?
choices: Is liked by learners / is not liked by learners
Is big / is small
Has wings / has no wings
Looks beautiful / does not look beautiful
quiz.rationale: A key needs paired statements that are observable and clear, so any user gets the same answer. 'Has wings / no wings' can be checked by anyone. Beauty, size and liking are opinions or vary between people.
quiz.placement: Final classification challenge, Task 2: build or complete a dichotomous key for at least 6 organisms and exchange it with another group

quiz.prompt: A learner writes: 'Maize has one cotyledon and parallel veins, but bean has two cotyledons and net veins.' Which reasoning best explains why this evidence helps to classify them accurately?
choices: Any learner can observe and check these features, so everyone gets the same groups
Maize is eaten more than bean, so it needs its own group
The teacher said that maize and bean are different, so they are
Maize is bigger than bean, so they must be separate groups
quiz.rationale: Good reasoning links evidence to the principle that shared, observable characteristics give the same grouping for any learner. Size, use as food and authority do not.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) answering 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?'

quiz.prompt: After sorting the Driving Question Board, a group wants to add a new question that goes beyond the classroom. Which question is the best fit?
choices: Which organism in our collection is the prettiest?
How can a dichotomous key help identify crop pests in Nakuru?
Why do we have a Driving Question Board?
Is a goat bigger than a chicken?
quiz.rationale: The best new question applies classification knowledge to a real situation such as farming and can be investigated. The others are opinions, simple comparisons or about classroom routine.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: writing at least one new question beyond the classroom

quiz.prompt: A learner finds a tilapia from Lake Victoria. It has a backbone, gills and fins. Where should the learner's final classification model place it?
choices: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Arthropoda
Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Birds
Kingdom Plantae, Division Spermatophyta
Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Fish
quiz.rationale: Animals with a backbone are in Phylum Chordata, and a fish with gills and fins belongs to the fish class. Arthropods lack a backbone, and birds are a different class of Chordata.
quiz.placement: Final model: 'Can your model place a new organism you have never seen, say a tilapia or a cypress tree?'

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the importance of viruses to Kenyans is correct?
choices: Viruses can cause diseases such as measles and maize streak, but are also used in vaccines and biotechnology
Viruses affect only people and never crops
Viruses make food for plants by photosynthesis
Viruses only cause disease and have no use
quiz.rationale: Viruses cause harm in health (for example measles) and agriculture (maize streak virus), but are also used in vaccines and biotechnology.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: importance of viruses in health, agriculture and biotechnology (one harm and one benefit)
